author: Mehrdad Kia

host_reactions.correct_generic: Dasatir. Purifiers were so eager to purge Arabic that they stuffed their essays with completely fabricated seventeenth-century fake words.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong Zoroastrian text. The forged compilation was the *Dasatir*.

clue_text: In 1870, Jalal al-Din Mirza published this three-volume textbook for Dar al-Fonun students, narrating Iranian history down to the Sasanian collapse in uncompromising pure Persian.
explanation: Printed in lithograph in Vienna and Tehran between 1868 and 1870, *Nameh-ye Khosravan* served as the pioneer secular textbook for Dar al-Fonun pupils, featuring engraved portraits of ancient Persian monarchs and demonstrating that history could be narrated without Arabic loans.
book_title: Persian Nationalism and the Campaign for Language Purification
author: Mehrdad Kia

host_reactions.correct_generic: Nameh-ye Khosravan. A textbook that taught schoolboys that the glories of Cyrus and Shapur could be recounted without a single Arabic word.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong textbook. Jalal al-Din Mirza authored *Nameh-ye Khosravan*.

clue_text: In 1872, this British major-general led the boundary commission that formally partitioned the historic province of Sistan between Iran and Afghanistan.
explanation: Major-General Sir Frederic Goldsmid drew the 'Goldsmid Line' in 1872, awarding the fertile left bank of the Helmand River to Afghanistan and leaving the arid right bank to Iran, cementing British imperial interests along the Indian frontier.

author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Major-General Sir Frederic Goldsmid. Drew a pencil line through the desert and severed the legendary homeland of Rostam in two.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong British arbitrator. Major-General Sir Frederic Goldsmid partitioned Sistan.

clue_text: The 1872 Goldsmid arbitration caused catastrophic ecological and political disputes by cutting the border across the vital delta of this great desert river.
explanation: The Helmand River (*Hirmand*) feeds the shallow Hamun lakes in the Sistan depression; Goldsmid's boundary divided the irrigation canals and river channels, leaving upstream control to Afghan amirs and causing chronic seasonal droughts in Iranian Sistan.
book_title: Fragile Frontiers: The Diminishing Domains of Qajar Iran
author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Helmand River. A life-giving desert waterway chopped in two by British cartographers, leaving downstream farmers to thirst for a century.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong river. The partition cut across the Helmand River.

clue_text: The partitioned province held deep national and mythological significance for Iranians as the historic home territory of this supreme hero of the *Shahnameh*.
explanation: In Qajar diplomatic notes and popular protests, Sistan was fiercely claimed as the sacred homeland of Rostam (*Zabolestan*), making its diplomatic truncation feel like a desecration of the very heart of the *Shahnameh*.
book_title: Fragile Frontiers: The Diminishing Domains of Qajar Iran
author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Rostam. British diplomats drew border lines through the heroic home of Rostam and couldn't understand why Iranians took it personally.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong mythological hero. Sistan was celebrated as the homeland of Rostam.

clue_text: This powerful hereditary ruler of Qa'inat and Sistan, titled Heshmat al-Molk, desperately mobilized local forces to defend Iranian sovereignty during the boundary crisis.
explanation: Amir Ali Akbar Khan (Amir Alam Khan / Heshmat al-Molk), the powerful hereditary lord of Birjand and Qa'inat, governed Iranian Sistan, warning Tehran that British commissions were deliberately handing irrigation weirs to Afghan tribes.
book_title: Fragile Frontiers: The Diminishing Domains of Qajar Iran
author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Amir Alam Khan. The desert lord of Birjand who watched British surveyors give away his family's canal networks with the stroke of a pen.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong border ruler. Amir Alam Khan (Heshmat al-Molk) governed Sistan.

clue_text: Between 1903 and 1905, this British colonial officer led a second massive boundary mission to Sistan, sparking widespread rioting when he altered water-allocation formulas.
explanation: Colonel Sir Henry McMahon led an enormous expedition with 1,500 troops and surveyors into Sistan between 1903 and 1905; his award allocating one-third of the Helmand flow to Iran provoked violent anti-British protests in Tehran and Sistan.
book_title: Fragile Frontiers: The Diminishing Domains of Qajar Iran
author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Sir Henry McMahon. Marched fifteen hundred men into the desert dust only to leave behind an even more bitter water war.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong British officer. Sir Henry McMahon led the 1903–1905 arbitration.

clue_text: During the late nineteenth century, this traditional Arabic loanword shifted from meaning one's local birth town or village to signifying the bounded, sacred national homeland of Iran.
explanation: As documented by Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet, *vatan* was transformed from a localized nostalgia for one's town into an emotive, patriotic symbol of the physical Iranian land with cartographic frontiers to be defended with blood.

author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Vatan. Turned an old word for one's home village into a sacred national map that citizens were expected to die for.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong conceptual term. The word was *Vatan*.

clue_text: Before the rise of modern territorial nationalism, the Qajar state designated its vast, loosely governed realm by this classical Persian imperial title.
explanation: The Qajar realm was formally titled *Mamalek-e Mahrusa-ye Iran* (The Guarded Domains of Iran), conceptualizing the empire not as a unified nation-state, but as a mosaic of autonomous provinces and tribal territories guarded by the Shah.
book_title: Picturing the homeland: geography and national identity in late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Iran
author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Mamalek-e Mahrusa-ye Iran. A patchwork empire of khans, tribes, and provinces held together by the Shah's umbrella rather than barbed-wire borders.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong imperial designation. The traditional title was *Mamalek-e Mahrusa-ye Iran*.

clue_text: This four-volume geographical and historical dictionary of Iran's cities and provinces, published in the 1870s, was authored by the court scholar E'temad os-Saltaneh.
explanation: Mohammad Hasan Khan E'temad os-Saltaneh published *Mir'at al-Buldan* (Mirror of the Lands) between 1877 and 1880, attempting an exhaustive encyclopedic gazetteer of every province, town, and fortress in Iran to define the physical boundaries of the realm.
book_title: Picturing the homeland: geography and national identity in late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Iran
author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Mir'at al-Buldan. Attempted to catalog every fortress, village, and melon patch in the country to prove to European cartographers that Iran was a real kingdom.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong geographical text. E'temad os-Saltaneh authored *Mir'at al-Buldan*.

clue_text: Founded in 1896 by Mohammad Hossein Foroughi, this premier weekly reformist newspaper was praised for publishing editorials that defined modern territorial geography as the basis of civic patriotism.
explanation: Mohammad Hossein Foroughi (Zoka al-Molk I) published *Tarbiyat* in Tehran from 1896 to 1907; it was Iran's first non-governmental paper to consistently publish articles arguing that love of country (*hubb al-vatan*) required deep scientific knowledge of national geography.

author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Tarbiyat. Foroughi's paper told readers that you cannot truly love your country if you don't even know where its borders are drawn.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong newspaper. The reformist weekly was *Tarbiyat*.

explanation: Published in three massive folio volumes between 1884 and 1886, *Matla al-Shams* traced the royal route to the shrine of Mashhad, recording Persian inscriptions, tombs, and historical borders across Khorasan to counter Russian expansion after the fall of Merv.

author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Matla al-Shams. Cataloged every shrine and tomb inscription in Khorasan to prove to the Tsar that the lands of the rising sun were eternally Iranian.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong geographical text. E'temad os-Saltaneh authored *Matla al-Shams*.

clue_text: Signed in 1847 following four agonizing years of mediation by Britain and Russia, this landmark treaty stabilized the southwestern border between Qajar Iran and the Ottoman Empire.
explanation: The Second Treaty of Erzurum (May 31, 1847) formally delineated the porous Ottoman-Iranian border, granting Iran undisputed sovereignty over the city and port of Mohammerah (Khorramshahr) and free navigation on the Shatt al-Arab.

author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong border treaty. The pact was the Second Treaty of Erzurum.

clue_text: The primary triumph of Iranian diplomacy at Erzurum was securing undisputed sovereignty over this strategic port city at the mouth of the Karun River, known then as Mohammerah.
explanation: The Ottoman governor of Baghdad, Ali Riza Pasha, had sacked Mohammerah in 1837; at the Erzurum conference, Iranian negotiators successfully repulsed all Ottoman claims and forced the Porte to recognize the city as Persian territory.
book_title: Fragile Frontiers: The Diminishing Domains of Qajar Iran
author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Khorramshahr. The Ottomans burned it to the ground in 1837, but Iranian diplomats won it back at the conference table.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong strategic port. Iranian diplomacy secured Khorramshahr (Mohammerah).

clue_text: Before rising to become Nasir al-Din Shah's celebrated prime minister, this master statesman spent nearly four years in Anatolia as Iran's chief negotiator at Erzurum.
explanation: Mirza Taqi Khan (later Amir Kabir) demonstrated iron will and astonishing diplomatic mastery during the 1843–1847 Erzurum conference, even surviving a deadly riot when a fanatic Turkish mob attacked his residence, killing several of his staff.
book_title: Fragile Frontiers: The Diminishing Domains of Qajar Iran
author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Mirza Taqi Khan. Dodged Turkish bayonets and mob stones in Erzurum to defend every inch of the Khuzestan frontier.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong statesman. Mirza Taqi Khan (Amir Kabir) conducted the negotiations.

clue_text: The central maritime dispute at Erzurum centered on anchorage and navigation rights along this border waterway formed by the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates.
explanation: The Ottomans claimed total monopoly over the entire width of the Shatt al-Arab (*Arvand Rud*) up to the low-water mark of the Iranian bank; the Treaty of Erzurum affirmed Iranian vessels had the permanent right to navigate the waterway freely.

author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Shatt al-Arab. The muddy waterway that saw more diplomatic ink spilled over its shipping channels than almost any river on earth.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong border waterway. The dispute concerned the Shatt al-Arab (Arvand Rud).

clue_text: Controversy erupted after the treaty was signed because British and Russian ambassadors coerced the Iranian envoy in Istanbul into signing this unilateral diplomatic addendum behind Amir Kabir's back.
explanation: Before ratifying the treaty, the Ottoman Porte demanded clarifications restricting Iranian rights on the Shatt; British and Russian envoys in Istanbul drafted the 'Explanatory Note' of 1847, pressuring Iran's ambassador Mirza Ja'far Khan Moshir al-Dawla into accepting it without the knowledge of Amir Kabir, who furiously rejected its validity.
book_title: Fragile Frontiers: The Diminishing Domains of Qajar Iran
author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: The Explanatory Note. British and Russian diplomats quietly ambushed the Iranian ambassador in Istanbul with a secret memo to undo Amir Kabir's hard-won victories.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong diplomatic addendum. The controversial document was the Explanatory Note.

clue_text: In December 1881, under intense pressure from St. Petersburg, Nasir al-Din Shah signed this convention that permanently ceded Transcaspian Turkmen territories to Russia.

author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: 1881 Akhal Boundary Convention. Signed away centuries of Persian frontier authority in Central Asia with a single imperial stroke of the pen.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong frontier treaty. The agreement was the 1881 Akhal Boundary Convention.

author: Firuz Kazemzadeh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Geok Tepe. Blew up the desert mud fortress with dynamite and massacred fifteen thousand people to clear the path to Iran's northeastern doorstep.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong desert fortress. Russian forces stormed Geok Tepe.

clue_text: Nicknamed the 'White General' for his white uniform and charger, this ruthless Russian imperial commander orchestrated the brutal siege and massacre at Geok Tepe.
explanation: General Mikhail Dmitrievich Skobelev (1843–1882) ordered his cavalry to pursue and mercilessly slaughter the fleeing population at Geok Tepe, famously declaring: 'The harder you hit them, the longer they stay quiet.'
book_title: Cambridge History of Iran, Vol. 7: From Nadir Shah to the Islamic Republic
author: Firuz Kazemzadeh

host_reactions.correct_generic: General Mikhail Skobelev. Wore a pristine white uniform while ordering the slaughter of every man, woman, and child who ran from the mud walls.

clue_text: In 1884, Russia extinguished centuries of Iranian historical suzerainty over Central Asia by bloodlessly annexing this legendary Silk Road oasis city.
explanation: In February 1884, Russian cavalry under General Komarov rode into Merv; the local elders surrendered without firing a shot, ending Iran's historic ties to the ancient eastern capital of Sanjar and creating diplomatic panic in London.

author: Firuz Kazemzadeh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Merv. An ancient Silk Road jewel swallowed by the Tsar's empire in an afternoon without firing a single pistol shot.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong oasis city. Russia annexed Merv in 1884.

explanation: Article I established that the frontier began at the Caspian Sea and ran up the Atrek River (*Rud-e Atrak*) eastward to the mountains, permanently fixing the boundary that still divides Iran and Turkmenistan today.

author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Atrek River. Marked the line in the desert mud where the Russian Empire ended and the Qajar kingdom began.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong border river. The border was fixed along the Atrek River.

clue_text: Commanding the Persian Cossack Brigade from 1894 to 1903, this iron-willed Russian colonel purged corrupt officers and forged the unit into the most disciplined force in Iran.
explanation: Colonel Vladimir Andreevich Kosagovskii took command of a near-mutinous brigade in 1894; he dismissed corrupt Qajar commanders, ensured prompt payment of wages, and built the unit into the sole reliable armed force in the capital.

author: Firuz Kazemzadeh

author: Firuz Kazemzadeh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Maidan-e Mashq. The dusty training ground where Russian officers taught Persian recruits how to jump wooden hurdles and charge with drawn sabres.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong square. The drills were conducted at the Maidan-e Mashq.

clue_text: In July 1872, the Qajar government signed a breathtaking concession granting this British financier exclusive rights to build all railways, extract all mines, and control all forests in Iran.

host_reactions.correct_generic: Baron Julius de Reuter. Was handed the deed to an entire kingdom's economic resources for a token advance and a few polite promises.

explanation: Mirza Malkam Khan founded the *Faramushkhaneh* (House of Oblivion or Freemason Lodge) in 1858, modeled after the French Grand Orient; attracting royal princes and students of the Dar al-Fonun, it was banned by the Shah in October 1861 for spreading republican and anti-monarchical ideas.

host_reactions.correct_generic: Faramushkhaneh. The Shah thought it was a gentleman's club until he realized his own cousins were inside debating whether Iran needed a king at all.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong proto-Masonic lodge. The society was the Faramushkhaneh.

explanation: *Kaveh*, founded in Berlin in 1916 by Sayyid Hasan Taqizadeh and Mohammad-Ali Jamalzadeh with German backing, used the mythical figure of Kaveh the Blacksmith (*Kaveh-ye Ahangar*) to champion national liberation, pure Persian scholarship, and modernization.

explanation: Iran was on the silver standard (*qiran*); when Western nations abandoned bimetallism for the gold standard between 1873 and 1900, the global price of silver plummeted by over 50%, devastating Iran's foreign exchange rates, exploding the cost of imports, and driving runaway inflation.

author: Ervand Abrahamian

host_reactions.correct_generic: Silver. Western banks hoarded gold, and every month the silver coins in an Iranian merchant's pocket bought less and less.

explanation: The Imperial Bank of Persia (*Bank-e Shahi-ye Iran*), founded by Reuter in 1889 with headquarters in London and Tehran, received a sixty-year monopoly on issuing paper currency (scrip) across Iran, functioning as the country's de facto central bank.

author: Ervand Abrahamian

host_reactions.correct_generic: The Imperial Bank of Persia. A British corporation held the sole legal right to run the printing presses that printed Iranian paper money.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong banking institution. The note-issuing bank was the Imperial Bank of Persia.

explanation: The *Banque d'Escompte de Perse* (Bank-e Esteqrazi), established in 1890 and taken over by the Russian Ministry of Finance in 1897, deliberately loaned millions of rubles to Iranian princes, ministers, and the royal court, mortgaging state customs and estates as collateral.

author: Ervand Abrahamian

host_reactions.correct_generic: Banque d'Escompte de Perse. Trapped the entire Qajar ruling class in debt and used unpaid promissory notes as diplomatic weapons.

explanation: Hajji Mohammad Hasan Amin al-Zarb (1835–1898), the wealthiest merchant in Iran, petitioned the Shah in 1879 with a blueprint for a national bank (*Bank-e Melli*) capitalized by Iranian merchants to finance railways and mining, but the court ignored his proposal in favor of foreign loans.

author: Ervand Abrahamian

author: Mansour Bonakdarian

author: Mansour Bonakdarian

host_reactions.correct_generic: Government Gendarmerie. Swedish captains taught Iranian cadets Prussian drill until the First World War scattered them all across the Ottoman border.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You said the Cossacks. This force was the Majlis's own answer to them, stood up in 1910 and handed to Stockholm.

clue_text: Appointed in 1911 as the first Commandant of the Government Gendarmerie, this Swedish general built the force up to seven provincial regiments.
explanation: General Harald Hjalmarson established rigorous officer academies in Tehran and conciliated the ulama to build public trust in the force.
book_title: Anglo-Iranian Relations since 1800
author: Stephanie Cronin

host_reactions.correct_generic: General Hjalmarson. Left chilly Stockholm to chase tribal highwaymen through the Fars gorges.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the man who took it over years later. The first commandant was the one who founded the academies and courted the clergy.

clue_text: In November 1915, this patriotic gendarme major seized control of Shiraz, arrested British consular staff, and aligned Fars with the Central Powers.
explanation: Major Ali Quli Khan Pasyan carried out the nationalist takeover in Shiraz, impounding the Imperial Bank and holding British officials hostage in Tangistan.
book_title: Anglo-Iranian Relations since 1800
author: Stephanie Cronin

host_reactions.correct_generic: Major Ali Quli Khan Pasyan. Turned British Armstrong guns onto the British consulate gates that had paid for them.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a foreign officer. The major who took Shiraz in November 1915 was Persian, wearing a gendarme uniform.

clue_text: Following the 1917 reorganization, this Swedish officer was retained by Prime Minister Vosuq al-Dowleh as Commandant of the reconstituted Gendarmerie.
explanation: Colonel Gleerup oversaw the rapid expansion of the Gendarmerie to nearly 10,000 men prior to the 1921 coup.
book_title: Anglo-Iranian Relations since 1800
author: Stephanie Cronin

host_reactions.correct_generic: Colonel Per Gleerup. Commanded ten thousand Iranian gendarmes with just two Swedish comrades left beside his command desk.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the man who founded it. This one was kept on after the 1917 overhaul, and the force nearly doubled under him.

category: SAVE THE DATE, REGRET THE EVENT
clue_text: In spring 1916, this Iranian gendarme captain was bought over by Qavam al-Mulk's agents to stage a counter-coup that restored Shiraz to British control.
explanation: Fath al-Mulk used British funding and won over NCOs to overthrow the nationalist gendarme committee, paving the way for Sykes's South Persia Rifles.
book_title: Anglo-Iranian Relations since 1800
author: Stephanie Cronin

host_reactions.correct_generic: Captain Fath al-Mulk. Discovered that British bank notes in Shiraz were far more convincing than German anti-imperialist brochures.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a British officer. The captain who undid the nationalist committee in Shiraz wore the same uniform as the men he arrested.

clue_text: Arrested in May 1937 under Reza Shah's anti-communist dragnet, this group of prominent left-wing intellectuals later formed the nucleus of the Tudeh Party.
explanation: The Group of 53 was prosecuted under the 1931 Anti-Collectivist Law; after their release in 1941, surviving members founded the Tudeh Party.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: M. Reza Ghods

host_reactions.correct_generic: Group of 53. Fifty-three intellectuals entered Qasr Prison reading Das Kapital and came out in 1941 to run the largest party in the Middle East.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a party. What the dragnet in 1937 caught was a circle of intellectuals who were not organized as anything yet.

clue_text: Educated in chemistry in Berlin, this Marxist theoretician founded the intellectual journal Dunya in 1934 and died in prison in 1940.
explanation: Dr. Taghi Arani introduced dialectical materialism to Iranian readers through Dunya and became a martyr figure for the Iranian socialist movement.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: M. Reza Ghods

host_reactions.correct_generic: Taghi Arani. Studied quantum chemistry in Berlin to explain historical materialism to prisoners in Tehran.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named his journal. I wanted the man behind it, the Berlin-trained scientist who died in a cell in 1940.

clue_text: Passed in June 1931, this stringent penal statute outlawed any organization advocating collectivist or communist doctrines undermining state security.
accepted_aliases: قانون مجازات مقدمین علیه امنیت کشور
explanation: The 1931 legislation targeted the remnants of the Communist Party and labor unions, providing the legal basis to arrest Arani's circle in 1937.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: M. Reza Ghods

host_reactions.correct_generic: Anti-Collectivist Law of 1931. Made thinking about property redistribution a ticket to ten years behind bars.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You cited a sedition act from the war years. The statute that put Arani's circle in the dock was passed in 1931.

clue_text: Inaugurated in 1929 on the site of a Qajar hunting pavilion, this modern radial penitentiary in Tehran held the Group of 53 and countless political dissidents.
explanation: Built by the Russian-born architect Nikolai Markov, Qasr Prison was Iran's first modern centralized correctional institution.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: M. Reza Ghods

host_reactions.correct_generic: Qasr Prison. Designed as a modern reformatory where the Shah's chief of police could invent creative new ways to administer lethal air injections.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a fortress in the provinces. The prison that held the Group of 53 stood on an old royal hunting ground in the capital.

clue_text: This Azerbaijani communist, who edited Horriyat in 1919, spent ten years imprisoned in Qasr before reemerging in 1945 to lead an autonomous regime in Tabriz.
explanation: Pishevari was arrested in December 1930 and kept in Qasr and Kashan until 1941, later founding the Azerbaijan Democratic Party.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: M. Reza Ghods

host_reactions.correct_generic: Jafar Pishevari. Survived ten years in the Shah's cells only to flee to Baku and die in a suspicious automobile crash in Soviet exile.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a cleric. The man who spent ten years in Qasr and then surfaced in Tabriz in 1945 had been editing a newspaper back in 1919.

clue_text: Triggered by wartime food shortages and political maneuvering, this December 1942 riot saw crowds sack Baharistan Square and commercial districts.
explanation: The December 1942 bread riot resulted from artificial grain shortages and political factionalism under Allied military occupation.
book_title: International Journal of Middle East Studies
author: Stephen L. McFarland

host_reactions.correct_generic: Tehran Bread Riot of 1942. Starving crowds demanded flour while political factions weaponized their hunger against the premier.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You called it a general strike. This one was over the price of a loaf, and it emptied out Baharistan Square in December.

clue_text: Serving as Prime Minister during the 1942 bread riot, this veteran statesman saw his private residence attacked and looted by the mob.
explanation: Ahmad Qavam believed the riots were orchestrated by court loyalists and military officers seeking to oust his cabinet.
book_title: International Journal of Middle East Studies
author: Stephen L. McFarland

host_reactions.correct_generic: Ahmad Qavam. Survived the sacking of his own dining room to outmaneuver Stalin in Moscow in the Kremlin in 1946.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a military man. The prime minister who watched the crowd sack his own residence over bread later blamed the palace for it.

clue_text: Wartime reports on the Tehran bread riot highlighted the mobilization of these traditional knife-wielding neighborhood toughs by elite political conspirators.
explanation: The chaqukeshan were mobilized by right-wing politicians and court figures to turn a student demonstration into a destructive riot.
book_title: International Journal of Middle East Studies
author: Stephen L. McFarland

host_reactions.correct_generic: Chaqukeshan. Turned political muscle into a commodity for rent to the highest royalist bidder.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You said the army. The strong-arm men who turned a student march into a riot were hired off the street, and they came with their own blades.

clue_text: In November 1942, the Majlis passed legislation re-hiring this American financial adviser as Director General of Finance with sweeping executive powers.
explanation: Arthur Millspaugh returned to Iran in 1942 to head financial stabilization and grain distribution, but soon clashed with nationalist deputies and the cabinet.
book_title: International Journal of Middle East Studies
author: Stephen L. McFarland

host_reactions.correct_generic: Arthur Millspaugh. Believed American accounting methods could fix wartime famine in a country occupied by two foreign armies.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named his successor. The American the Majlis recalled in November 1942 had already run Iranian finances once, back in the twenties.

clue_text: Appointed in 1942 to administer food supplies and civilian road transport in Iran, this American adviser was blamed by Qavam for exacerbating the bread crisis.
explanation: Sheridan struggled to commandeer trucks monopolized by the UK Commercial Corporation, leaving wheat shipments stranded while Tehran bakeries ran dry.
book_title: International Journal of Middle East Studies
author: Stephen L. McFarland

host_reactions.correct_generic: James Sheridan. Tried to deliver grain to Tehran bakeries without trucks, only to find the British army had requisitioned every wheel.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the treasurer-general. This American was hired for food and trucks, not money, and Qavam laid the empty bakeries at his feet.

clue_text: Launched on 25 August 1941, this joint military invasion by Great Britain and the Soviet Union shattered Iranian neutrality and forced Reza Shah's abdication.
explanation: Codenamed Operation Countenance, the invasion aimed to secure the Trans-Iranian supply corridor to the USSR and protect Anglo-Iranian oil fields.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: F. Eshraghi

host_reactions.correct_generic: Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran. Swept away sixteen years of militarist modernization in seventy-two hours of border skirmishes.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You gave me a corridor. The August 1941 operation was a two-front invasion, and it finished the man on the throne for good.

clue_text: Prime Minister when Allied forces crossed the borders in August 1941, this loyal bureaucrat resigned within days as his military options vanished.
explanation: Ali Mansur attempted to pursue diplomatic neutrality but was cast aside by Reza Shah in favor of Mohammad Ali Foroughi to negotiate the surrender.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: F. Eshraghi

host_reactions.correct_generic: Ali Mansur. Read the Allied ultimatum to parliament in the morning and handed his resignation to the palace by afternoon.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the man who cleaned up after. The premier who resigned within days, in August 1941, was a loyal bureaucrat with no army left to command.

clue_text: Directing Allied invasion strategy from his headquarters at Simla in India, this British Commander-in-Chief ordered the dual-column thrust into southern Iran.
explanation: General Wavell oversaw operations to secure the Khuzestan oilfields and naval facilities at Khorramshahr and Bandar Shahpur.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: F. Eshraghi

host_reactions.correct_generic: General Archibald Wavell. Plotted the invasion of neutral Iran from the cool comfort of a British hill station in India.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a field commander. The orders came from a desk in India, from the man responsible for the whole theater.

clue_text: As General Officer Commanding British troops in Iraq (Iraq Command), this lieutenant-general drew up the tactical plans to assault Abadan and Ahwaz.
explanation: Quinan commanded Paiforce (Persia and Iraq Force), supervising the landing of Indian troops at Abadan and the push toward Kermanshah.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: F. Eshraghi

host_reactions.correct_generic: Lieutenant-General E. P. Quinan. Rehearsed the seizure of the world's largest oil refinery on sand tables in Basra.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the theater commander. The man who actually drew the plan for Abadan and Ahwaz was a lieutenant-general working out of Iraq.

clue_text: On the opening day of the August 1941 invasion, British forces immediately seized this small border oil field located south of Khanaqin.
explanation: The Naft-i-Shah field was connected by pipeline to the Kermanshah refinery, making it a critical strategic target for securing Allied fuel in western Iran.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: F. Eshraghi

host_reactions.correct_generic: Naft-i-Shah. Secured before breakfast on day one so British tanks would have petrol to drive to Kermanshah.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the big refinery. This was a small field south of Khanaqin, and a pipeline ran from it straight to a refinery in the west.

clue_text: Erupting in late 1945 when the Red Army shielded separatist regimes in Tabriz and Mahabad, this standoff marked the first diplomatic crisis of the Cold War.
explanation: The crisis concluded after Premier Ahmad Qavam combined shrewd diplomacy in Moscow with an appeal to the newly established United Nations.
book_title: Iranian Studies
author: Louise Fawcett

host_reactions.correct_generic: Iran crisis of 1946. Proved that a small country with clever diplomats could use the UN charter to push the Red Army back across the Aras.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the Berlin blockade. This one started when the Red Army kept a separatist regime standing in Tabriz, and it was the first real scramble of the Cold War.

clue_text: As Iranian ambassador in Washington, this staunch diplomat presented Iran's formal complaint against the Soviet Union to the UN Security Council in early 1946.
explanation: Hussein Ala persistently kept the Iranian complaint on the Security Council agenda despite intense pressure from Soviet representative Andrei Gromyko.
book_title: Iranian Studies
author: Louise Fawcett

host_reactions.correct_generic: Hussein Ala. Stood at the UN microphone in New York while Soviet delegates staged the world's first diplomatic walkout.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the premier. The voice that kept the Iranian complaint on the table in New York belonged to a career diplomat, not to a politician back home.

clue_text: Signed in Tehran on 4 April 1946, this agreement promised Soviet troop withdrawal within six weeks in exchange for a proposed joint oil company.
explanation: Ahmad Qavam offered a 51% Soviet stake in a northern oil concession, but made its implementation subject to approval by the next parliament, which promptly rejected it.
book_title: Iranian Studies
author: Louise Fawcett

host_reactions.correct_generic: Qavam-Sadchikov Agreement. Exchanged five northern provinces today for a promise of Caspian oil that evaporated tomorrow.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the treaty from 1921. This deal was struck in Tehran in 1946, oil against promises, and the parliament had the last word.

clue_text: Adopted on 30 January 1946, this United Nations Security Council resolution was the very first substantive resolution passed by the council, addressing the Iranian question.
explanation: Resolutions 2 and 3 mandated that Moscow and Tehran resolve their dispute through direct talks while keeping the Security Council continuously informed.
book_title: Iranian Studies
author: Louise Fawcett

host_reactions.correct_generic: UN Security Council Resolution 2. The United Nations was less than a month old when it had to decide whether the Red Army was leaving Tabriz.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You handed me the Charter. This was the first substantive resolution the council ever produced, passed at the end of January 1946.

clue_text: Arriving in Tehran in March 1946 as the new Soviet ambassador, this diplomat signed the ill-fated oil joint-venture accord with Qavam.
explanation: Sadchikov was sent to secure oil rights after Qavam's talks in Moscow stalled, only to see the resulting draft agreement discarded once Soviet soldiers departed.
book_title: Iranian Studies
author: Louise Fawcett

host_reactions.correct_generic: Ivan Sadchikov. Shook hands on a 50-year oil concession and lived to watch the Iranian parliament vote it down 102 to 2.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named Molotov. The man who actually turned up in Tehran in March 1946 with the draft in his briefcase was a mere ambassador.

clue_text: Beginning with Tsarist claims and renewed in 1944 by Moscow, this coveted commercial prize in five Caspian provinces sparked intense political warfare in Tehran.
explanation: The northern oil concession in Gilan, Mazandaran, Gorgan, Khorasan, and Azerbaijan was vigorously pursued by the USSR to match British holdings in the south.
book_title: Oriente Moderno
author: James Clark

host_reactions.correct_generic: Northern oil concession. Moscow assumed that if London pumped barrels from Khuzestan, Soviet drills were entitled to Caspian sands.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a pipeline. This was a concession, five provinces on the Caspian, and it had been sitting in the file since the Tsars.

clue_text: In September 1944, this Soviet Vice-Commissar for Foreign Affairs arrived in Tehran to aggressively demand an immediate oil concession in northern Iran.
explanation: Kavtaradze held hostile press conferences in Tehran denouncing Prime Minister Mohammad Sa'ed after the Iranian cabinet refused to negotiate during foreign military occupation.
book_title: Oriente Moderno
author: James Clark

host_reactions.correct_generic: Sergei Kavtaradze. Brought an oil contract from Moscow and was genuinely bewildered when an occupied parliament declined to sign it.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the ambassador. The man who came to Tehran in September 1944 and blew up at the press was a vice-commissar from Moscow, sent to twist arms.

clue_text: In December 1944, this future Prime Minister authored a historic single-article law forbidding any Iranian official from discussing foreign oil concessions during wartime.
explanation: Mosaddeq's Negative Equilibrium doctrine held that granting oil to the Soviets to balance the British was suicidal, championing total refusal of concessions to both.
book_title: Oriente Moderno
author: James Clark

host_reactions.correct_generic: Mohammad Mosaddeq. Decided that the best answer to Soviet oil demands was a law making it a crime for ministers to even listen.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a leftist deputy. The one-article law that barred any wartime concession talk came from a future prime minister, and he was building a doctrine out of it.

clue_text: This Iranian Prime Minister bravely refused Kavtaradze's demand for northern oil in autumn 1944, provoking Soviet retaliation that forced his cabinet out of office.
explanation: Sa'ed was a former ambassador to Moscow whose firm refusal to sign concessions under military occupation earned him public praise but cost him the premiership.
book_title: Oriente Moderno
author: James Clark

host_reactions.correct_generic: Mohammad Sa'ed Maraghei. Told the Kremlin that oil talks would have to wait until Russian boots were off Iranian soil.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named Qavam. The premier who told Kavtaradze no in autumn 1944 lost his cabinet for it, and the country cheered him on the way out.

clue_text: On 22 October 1947, this parliament formally buried Soviet oil ambitions by voting overwhelmingly to invalidate the Qavam-Sadchikov agreement.
explanation: The single-article resolution passed by the Fifteenth Majlis not only nullified the northern pact but mandated that Iran reassert its rights in the south, planting the seeds for 1951 nationalization.
book_title: Oriente Moderno
author: James Clark

host_reactions.correct_generic: Fifteenth Majlis. Rejected Moscow's oil treaty with a 102-vote landslide and dared Stalin to do something about it.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the Senate. The chamber that buried the northern oil pact in October 1947 was the one elected on the promise to do it.

clue_text: Inaugurated on 31 March 1949 with an address by President Truman, this international broadcasting division promoted American culture and capitalism to Iranian listeners.
explanation: The VOA Persian service served as the ideological vanguard of Truman's 'liberal developmentalism', countering Soviet radio propaganda during the early Cold War.
book_title: Intelligence and National Security
author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: Voice of America Persian Service. Harry Truman went on the airwaves in 1949 to tell Tehran that American capitalism was their true friend.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the BBC. The service launched on the last day of March 1949 with an American president warming up the microphone.

clue_text: Extensively championed by VOA broadcasts in Iran, this Truman administration technical assistance initiative funded rural agriculture, public health, and literacy projects.
explanation: Iran was the first country to sign a Point Four technical assistance agreement with the United States in October 1950 under Prime Minister Razmara.
book_title: Intelligence and National Security
author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: Point Four program. Handed out tractors and DDT sprayers to Iranian peasants in hopes they would forget about Karl Marx.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the Marshall Plan. This one was about wells, seeds and literacy in the villages, not rebuilding factories in Europe.

clue_text: Established in 1953 to consolidate American overseas information activities, this agency oversaw VOA operations and operated reading rooms and libraries across Iran.
explanation: The United States Information Agency operated as the United States Information Service (USIS) overseas, running cultural centers and mobile cinema units in provincial Iranian towns.
book_title: Intelligence and National Security
author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: United States Information Agency. Screened Hollywood documentaries and distributed English paperbacks to show Tehran students how wonderful democracy was.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named the CIA. The outfit running those reading rooms and mobile cinemas was a public diplomacy agency, stood up in 1953.

clue_text: Serving as US ambassador to Iran from 1951 to 1954, this career diplomat warned Washington that VOA broadcasts were failing to stem the tide of nationalist anti-imperialism.
explanation: Loy Henderson was a Soviet specialist who viewed Mosaddeq as vulnerable to communist manipulation and ultimately coordinated with the CIA during the 1953 coup.
book_title: Intelligence and National Security
author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: Loy Henderson. Advised Washington that playing jazz records on the radio would not make Iranians forgive British oil profits.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a junior officer. The ambassador sending those bleak cables in the early fifties had been watching Moscow for a living.

clue_text: As Chief of the State Department's International Broadcasting Division from 1949 to 1952, this diplomat directed the massive expansion of VOA transmissions into Iran.
explanation: Kohler argued that radio was America's primary tool to win Iranian public opinion away from the Tudeh Party's radio network.
book_title: Intelligence and National Security
author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: Foy Kohler. Stationed shortwave relay towers around the Persian Gulf to make sure Voice of America could out-shout Radio Moscow.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a broadcaster. The man running that division from 1949 was a diplomat, and he treated the airwaves like a battlefield.

clue_text: Operating secretly inside the Iranian armed forces from 1944 until its sensational exposure in 1954, this clandestine network comprised hundreds of communist officers.
accepted_aliases: Military Organization of the Tudeh Party
explanation: The Tudeh Military Network included over 600 officers, including colonels and pilots, before its discovery led to mass executions in 1954-1955.

author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.correct_generic: Tudeh Military Network. Six hundred officers had Marx in their footlockers and waited for orders from a central committee that never sent them.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You heard 'clandestine' and reached straight for the embassy. The red thread ran through the officer corps, and you never once looked at a uniform.

clue_text: A leading Marxist theoretician and architect, this radical headed the hardline faction of the Tudeh Executive Committee that favored an aggressive posture during the 1953 coup.
explanation: Kianouri maintained secret contacts with Mosaddeq during the crisis, but factional division paralyzed the party on 19 August 1953.
book_title: International Journal of Middle East Studies
author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.correct_generic: Noureddin Kianouri. Designed modernist houses in Tehran while designing theoretical revolutions for the working class.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You wanted a man with a slide rule. The hardliners kept an architect, and he was not the one you named.

clue_text: A legendary communist artillery captain and mathematical prodigy, this head of the Tudeh Military Network evaded police for years before his 1957 capture and execution.
explanation: Roozbeh escaped from prison multiple times and directed clandestine party operations until wounded in a shootout in southern Tehran in 1957.
book_title: International Journal of Middle East Studies
author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.correct_generic: Khosro Roozbeh. Escaped prison twice disguised as a guard and wrote geometry manuals in his underground hideouts.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: An artillery captain who outran the police for years, and you could not place him. At least the math prodigy could count your mistakes.

clue_text: Serving as First Secretary of the Tudeh Party during the oil nationalization crisis, this theoretical physicist led the moderate faction from abroad.
explanation: Radmanesh served as First Secretary from 1948 until 1969, presiding over decades of acrimonious ideological factionalism in Leipzig and Moscow.
book_title: International Journal of Middle East Studies
author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.correct_generic: Reza Radmanesh. Held a doctorate in mathematical physics from Paris to spend twenty years refereeing arguments between exiled Marxists in East Germany.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Twenty years in the chair and you could not hold the name. The party's physicist is not amused.

clue_text: This military prosecutor and police investigator uncovered the Tudeh Military Network in August 1954 after discovering a telltale notebook left behind by an arrestee.
explanation: Colonel Sorkhi's accidental discovery led directly to the arrest of hundreds of officers and cemented Teymour Bakhtiar's reputation as Military Governor.
book_title: International Journal of Middle East Studies
author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.correct_generic: Mohammad Baqer Sorkhi. A single coded address book in his hands brought down six hundred officers and destroyed the party's military wing.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: A stray notebook cracked the whole network and you credited the wrong investigator. Even the arrested man did more homework than you.

clue_text: Codenamed TP-AJAX by the CIA and Operation Boot by MI6, this joint covert operation overthrew Mohammad Mosaddeq in August 1953.
explanation: Operation Ajax represented the first covert action authorized by the US government to overthrow a democratically elected sovereign foreign leader.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Operation Ajax. The CIA's first venture into regime change, executed with fake news, street mobs, and suitcases of crisp bank notes.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: TP-AJAX and Boot, and you invented a third. The file keeps two codenames and you produced neither.

clue_text: Grandson of President Theodore Roosevelt, this CIA station chief directed field operations for the 1953 coup from the US embassy compound in Tehran.
explanation: Roosevelt slipped into Tehran under an alias and coordinated with Iranian royalist networks after the initial coup attempt failed on 15 August 1953.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Kermit Roosevelt Jr. Slumped on the floor of a Buick in Tehran while engineering the fall of a constitutional prime minister.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: A Roosevelt inside the embassy and you could not smell the dynasty. Teddy's grandson ran the field and you handed me a stranger.

clue_text: A prominent architectural historian and Princeton scholar, this CIA covert operative co-drafted the operational plan for the 1953 coup and authored its leaked secret history.
explanation: Dr. Donald Wilber utilized his expertise in Persian architecture and language to craft propaganda tracts and orchestrate anti-Mosaddeq messaging.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Donald Wilber. Wrote scholarly monographs on Ilkhanid minarets and operational plans for overthrowing prime ministers.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You wanted a spook in a trench coat and missed the man with a Princeton chair. The coup was drafted by an art historian, of all people.

clue_text: Approved in April 1950, this landmark National Security Council directive formally globalized US containment policy and shaped Washington's zero-sum view of Iran.
explanation: Drafted under Paul Nitze, NSC 68 framed any communist gain along the Eurasian periphery as a catastrophic defeat for Western security.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: NSC 68. Fifty-eight pages of Cold War panic that convinced Washington the loss of any single oil well was the loss of the free world.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: April 1950 and a number, and you gave me a speech. Containment got its blueprint from a directive, not a radio address.

clue_text: Operating from Nicosia, this veteran MI6 station chief directed the British intelligence network in Iran and co-drafted the original coup blueprint with Donald Wilber.
explanation: Darbyshire managed the covert financing of the Rashidian brothers network from Cyprus after the British embassy in Tehran was shut down.
book_title: Middle Eastern Studies
author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Norman Darbyshire. Sat in Cyprus passing British gold to Iranian agents after Mosaddeq threw his embassy out of Tehran.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You looked in London and the man was on Cyprus. The service kept its Iran desk by the Mediterranean and you never left Whitehall.

clue_text: Proposed in late 1951 by Britain, the US, France, and Turkey, this regional defense organization sought to bind Arab states and Iran into Western security architecture.
explanation: The Middle East Command proposal foundered due to Egyptian nationalist rejection over the Suez Canal base and Iranian preoccupation with the oil crisis.
book_title: The International History Review
author: H. W. Brands

host_reactions.correct_generic: Middle East Command. Western diplomats drew military arrows across maps of Cairo and Tehran while both capitals were busy expelling British garrisons.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You gave me a treaty that never existed. Four powers floated a command and Cairo killed it before it drew a breath.

clue_text: As US Secretary of State under Truman, this diplomat repeatedly clashed with London by counseling restraint and urging concessions to Mosaddeq.
explanation: Acheson dispatched Averell Harriman to mediate the oil dispute, fearing that British intransigence would push Iran into Soviet arms.
book_title: The International History Review
author: H. W. Brands

host_reactions.correct_generic: Dean Acheson. Told the British Foreign Office that invading Abadan in 1951 would start World War III over a barrel of bunker fuel.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: You named a man who never sat in Truman's cabinet. The Secretary of State who fought London over restraint was sitting right there.

clue_text: Returning as British Foreign Secretary in Churchill's 1951 cabinet, this Tory statesman took an unyielding line against Mosaddeq and urged Washington to join a coup.
explanation: Anthony Eden viewed compromise with Mosaddeq as fatal to British prestige across the Middle East, working diligently to bring the incoming Eisenhower administration on board for regime change.
book_title: The International History Review
author: H. W. Brands

host_reactions.correct_generic: Anthony Eden. Convinced himself that conceding an oil refinery to Iran would cause the entire British Empire to unravel.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Churchill's return brought a hardliner back to the Foreign Office, and you named someone else. The Tories had exactly one man this unforgiving.

clue_text: London's confrontation with Iranian oil nationalization was heavily conditioned by simultaneous armed clashes around this massive British military enclave in Egypt.
explanation: British officials feared that yielding to Mosaddeq in Abadan would embolden Egyptian nationalists demanding the total evacuation of 80,000 British troops from the Suez base.

category: THE REDS HAVE LEFT THE BUILDING
clue_text: The Soviet leader whom the Iranian envoy met on 19 December 1920, and who told him of the plan to post a Soviet minister to Tehran.

clue_text: The disruption of the Iranian oil industry in 1951 threatened the readiness of this British fighting service, which drew eighty-five per cent of its furnace oil from the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company.

author: H. W. Brands

host_reactions.correct_generic: Royal Navy. A fleet that sailed on other people's oil.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. That service could not keep its boilers lit without Abadan.

clue_text: The British chiefs of staff reported this proposal for invading the island of Abadan to Clement Attlee's Labour cabinet; it would have required up to 70,000 troops, two cruisers and a wing of fighter planes.
explanation: Plan Y was the British military blueprint for seizing Abadan and the oil installations after Iran nationalized the AIOC.
book_title: The International History Review
author: H. W. Brands

host_reactions.correct_generic: Plan Y. The Empire's last roar, aimed at an island.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong. The chiefs of staff had this one planned down to the landing craft.

clue_text: Dean Acheson wrote of this Labour foreign secretary that he knew nothing of foreign affairs and had no feel for situations beyond the sound of Bow bells.
explanation: Acheson's acid assessment of Herbert Morrison captured the low American regard for Britain's handling of the oil crisis.
book_title: The International History Review
author: H. W. Brands

host_reactions.correct_generic: Herbert Morrison. Bow bells and nothing past them.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. Acheson was sneering at the man running the Foreign Office.

clue_text: Its designers serially called their proposed collective security arrangement the Middle East Command, the Middle East Command Organization, and finally this outfit, whose name shrank to a three-letter acronym.
explanation: MEDO was the proposed regional command meant to draw the United States into Middle East defence, its serial renaming tracking its shifting purposes.

author: H. W. Brands

host_reactions.correct_generic: Middle East Defence Organization. A committee in a treaty's clothing.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. This one was renamed three times before it ever existed.

clue_text: One of the last Senate isolationists, this North Dakotan told the pastor of Boston's Old North Church to brush up on his Revolutionary War code and hang two lanterns in the tower.
explanation: Senator William Langer's two-lantern warning mocked the push to entangle the United States in Middle East security commitments.

author: H. W. Brands

host_reactions.correct_generic: William Langer. Paul Revere's warning, repurposed for a treaty.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. This senator wanted two lanterns hung at the Old North Church.

clue_text: In December 1950 the Truman administration endorsed a concession settlement between this Arabian-American oil company and Saudi Arabia, setting a 50:50 profit-sharing precedent.

author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: ARAMCO. Set the going rate and ruined London's afternoon.

explanation: The Supplemental Oil Agreement of 17 July 1949 was the settlement that Iran's parliament then refused to ratify, reopening the crisis.

author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Supplemental Oil Agreement. Signed, then buried by a filibuster.

explanation: Ambassador Henry Grady blamed Razmara's murder on the prime minister's support for the oil settlement, underscoring how lethal the oil question had become.

author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Henry Grady. Blamed the politics, not the pistol.

explanation: Averell Harriman's July 1951 mission as Truman's Special Envoy failed to bridge the gap between London and Tehran.

author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Averell Harriman. Mediated the whole crisis into a stalemate.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. This envoy flew to Tehran and came back with nothing.

clue_text: By 1951 US pressure and the ARAMCO precedent had pushed the oil company to improve its offer to a level this chairman considered equivalent to a 50:50 split.
explanation: AIOC chairman Sir William Fraser regarded the improved 1951 terms as equivalent to 50:50, a concession he was reluctant to concede as such.

author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Sir William Fraser. Called 50:50 something else and hoped no one noticed.

explanation: Brigadier General H. Norman Schwarzkopf headed the US Mission to the Iranian Gendarmerie, one of the military missions Truman retained in Iran.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

explanation: Max Thornburg embodied the American push to industrialize Iran while minimizing direct government intervention.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: William W. Barrett. Third man in, still crusading.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

explanation: Sidney Glazier, the Farsi Service's first director, embodied the bureaucratic tussles over whether VOA should inform or fight communism.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: Sidney Glazier. Directed a radio desk and a turf war at once.

author: H. W. Brands

explanation: Ayatollah Kashani's fatua urging the faithful in the armed forces to join the struggle intensified the religious pressure of the oil crisis.

author: H. W. Brands

host_reactions.correct_generic: Ayatollah Kashani. Put a religious seal on a political fight.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. This cleric told soldiers to join the struggle.

author: H. W. Brands

author: H. W. Brands

author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: Tudeh Party. The red scare with a Persian accent.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: Majlis. Wrote its own deadlock into American policy.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. This was the general who led the army mission, not the gendarmerie one.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: A second China. Because one was apparently not enough.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: Korea Roundup. A war bulletin with a hometown audience.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. This was the daily digest of a war three thousand miles away.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: John Taber. Saw a broadcast and reached for the budget knife.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

host_reactions.correct_generic: Ben Cherrington. Thought the cure might be the disease.

author: Deborah Kisatsky

author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. This was the assistant secretary who scolded the oil company.

author: Steve Marsh

host_reactions.correct_generic: Qavam al-Saltana. The spare premier nobody could install in time.

author: Steve Marsh

author: Willem M. Floor

author: Willem M. Floor

host_reactions.correct_generic: Waqf. Holy land, unholy rents.

author: Willem M. Floor

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong premier. His bill outlived your career.

author: Willem M. Floor

author: April R. Summitt

host_reactions.correct_generic: William Miller. Saw the Shah's distrust of Amini and wrote it down.

author: Maziar Behrooz

clue_text: Where the hard-liners insisted the Tudeh was the class party of the workers, the moderates billed it instead as this broader party of the labouring poor and other deprived classes.

explanation: The moderates called the Tudeh not the party of the working class but a toiler's party embracing other deprived classes.

author: Maziar Behrooz

clue_text: This hard-line ideologue, a professed Stalinist and dogmatic theorist, supplied the doctrinal fuel for the party's attacks on the nationalist government through 1951 and 1952.

clue_text: One of the faction's senior members, this man was no theorist but a party functionary whose chief asset was strong personal connections to the Soviets.
explanation: Kambakhsh was a party functionary with strong Soviet connections, not a theorist.

author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.correct_generic: Abdul Samad Kambakhsh. The Soviets liked him so well they made him the party's official friend of the Soviets.

author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.correct_generic: The Youth Organization. Under Sharmini it was a teenaged army with a radical slogan for every occasion.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong. Firouz ran the women and Quraishi the capital; this was the branch with the youngest members.

clue_text: Led by Maryam Firouz, the wife of a leading hard-liner, this party affiliate kept its post even as its youth counterpart was broken up.

author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.correct_generic: The Women's Organization. Maryam Firouz ran it, and being married to the faction's enforcer made her post untouchable.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. That was Sharmini's flock; the women's wing belonged to Firouz and nobody moved on it.

options: the Central Council of the United Trade Unions of Iranian Workers and Toilers

author: Maziar Behrooz

author: Maziar Behrooz

clue_text: In the minority on the executive committee, the hard-liners still held this capital-based nerve centre of the party network, run by Amanallah Quraishi.

author: Maziar Behrooz

clue_text: An economist and veteran party leader, this man broke with the Tudeh in 1948, taking his following into a socialist splinter the leadership never forgave.
explanation: Maleki led the 1948 split that came to be called the Third Force.
book_title: International Journal of Middle East Studies
author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.correct_generic: Khalil Maleki. He walked out in 1948 and spent the rest of his life being right at the worst possible moments.

clue_text: Held while the party reeled from the Azerbaijan crisis, this 1948 gathering hardened the two rival currents into factions with names and programmes.

explanation: The party's 1948 second congress gave the two factions their more definite shape.

author: Maziar Behrooz

clue_text: By the 1950s the socialist current that had quit the party under Khalil Maleki went by this three-word name, a bid to stand between the two Cold War camps.
explanation: The 1948 splinter under Maleki came to be called the Third Force.

author: Maziar Behrooz

clue_text: This moderate-faction member accused the Soviets of misusing the party's trust and admiration for the October revolution to impose their own line on the Tudeh.

author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.correct_generic: Fereydun Kishawarz. Called out Soviet meddling to the party's own face, which took nerve the moderates rarely showed.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. That was Sharmini, the maverick with a sidearm; Kishawarz was the one naming the interference.

category: THE REDS HAVE LEFT THE BUILDING
clue_text: Close to Beria and an architect of the 1945-46 Azerbaijan crisis, this man headed the Soviet republic's communist party and backed the hard-liners through his ally, the diplomat Rustam Aliev.

author: Maziar Behrooz

clue_text: The party's first secretary in the early 1950s, this man was one of three signatories of the first post-coup letter that blamed the hard-liners for the party's failure.

author: Maziar Behrooz

clue_text: A moderate on the executive committee, this man was the party's official liaison to its military wing, yet the hard-liners went around him and the tenth plenum later blamed him for it.

clue_text: Sympathetic to the moderates but too independent to join them, this executive-committee member wrote the second of the four post-coup letters, faulting both Sharmini and Kianuri.

author: Maziar Behrooz

host_reactions.wrong_generic: No. Bahrami and Judat headed the moderates; this was the committee's lone freelancer.

clue_text: In 1907 this popular Persian newspaper, which did much to shape the Iranian nationalist debate, declared patriotism a 'necessary duty', surpassing even one's commitment to life, property, and family.

author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

author: Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet

host_reactions.correct_generic: Amuzegar. Its remedy for a bad marriage was a schoolhouse, which is at least cheaper than a lawyer.

host_reactions.correct_generic: Farangistan. Printed in Berlin for an audience that would never be mistaken for a Tehrani crowd.

host_reactions.correct_generic: Parvin E'tisami. A poet plain enough that even the literary men admitted she could write.
